Source: http://www.marijuananews.com

Posted June 23, 2000 -- revised June 24, 2000
(MarijuanaNews note: The British Columbia Medical Association is holding its annual conference in Victoria next weekend. On Friday, June 30th, they will be voting on a variety of resolutions, one of which is about Canadian marijuana policies.

It is very disturbing in that it parrots the prohibitionist party line while ignoring the findings of fact of a variety of Canadian courts and even the DEAland Institute of Medicine report that is certainly not " pro-pot. "

In fact, the proposed resolution is an example of organized medicine’s overreaching arrogance in assuming that they are somehow experts on public policies that may impact on an individual’s health, which is their area of expertise.

Much worse, they ignore all of the evidence that contradicts their position. They are hardly unique in this.)


See
Column By Authors of the IOM Report On Medical Marijuana
Shows Why The Public Does Not Trust The Medical Establishment –
And Why They Should Not! With Analysis by Richard Cowan

From the BCMA Council on Health Promotion
Motions for presentation to the General Assembly
BCMA 2000 Annual General Meeting -- Friday, June 30, 2000
From the Addiction Medicine Committee

Resolution #2

Be it resolved that the BCMA urge the federal and provincial Ministers of Health that in any future parliamentary debate concerning changing the legal status of marijuana, the legislatures must take into account the serious effects of this drug on the physical, emotional and intellectual health of young people. Prevention of these serious health consequences in our youth is paramount.


(MarijuanaNews note: What does that last sentence mean? While protecting children is a moral imperative in any society, does " paramount " mean that all other considerations should be subordinated?

If so, then why do they not support alcohol and tobacco prohibition?

Obviously, there are other considerations that keep that rhetorical flourish from being consistently applied. For example, one might rightly conclude that alcohol prohibition was a social disaster, and even the BCMA would not recommend returning to it. [Various Canadian provinces tried alcohol prohibition before its southern neighbor.]

As we see, they really do not mean that " Prevention of these serious health consequences in our youth is paramount. " Nonetheless, protecting children should motivate everyone to take an honest look at the policies that work best.)

In view of recent debates about the use of marijuana by adult Canadians, it is important that the evidence on this drug be considered when deciding issues such as decriminalization or the use of " medical marijuana ".

(MarijuanaNews note: I find it curious and disturbing that they chose to put quotation marks around " medical marijuana. "

In a province with over a thousand people enrolled in one medical marijuana club, and in a country where there is overwhelming support for allowing the medical use of marijuana, do the doctors of the BCMA really have any doubts about marijuana’s medical value?

See
Chairman of the House of Lords Science and Technology Committee
Criticizes UK Government’s Rejection Of Report On Medical Marijuana
– 2 Articles With 2 of the Worst Prohibitionist Arguments
and
A Great Day For Medical Marijuana And Canadian Justice – Buyer For BC Compassion Club Gets Suspended Sentence for Possession of 13 Pounds -- Special to MarijuanaNews
and
Canadian Medical Association Journal Carries Favorable Article On Vancouver Compassion Club

And surely the BCMA does not mean to imply that the use of " medical marijuana " by the sick and dying should be subordinated to any supposed impact on adolescents. Or would they also suggest that the medical use of morphine and other dangerous and addictive drugs should be discontinued in deference to adolescents somehow being unable to understand the difference between medical and non-medical use of drugs?)
See
California Bureaucracy Suppresses Report Showing Marijuana Use Among California Students Leveled Off AfterPassage Of Prop 215. Meanwhile, In New Zealand, Prohibitionists Use The Same Party Line.

There is good evidence that marijuana is an addictive drug and that its use while driving or working has been shown to increase the likelihood of both motor vehicle accidents and work related accidents, some of them fatal.
(MarijuanaNews note: What does " addictive " mean? What are the implications for social policy, given that even caffeine is also an " addictive drug "? First, remember that this is from the " Addiction Medicine Committee. " Such a source makes this statement all the more disturbing. " Addictive " is a notoriously plastic term that tends to mean whatever the speaker wants it to mean. Here it seems to mean " Give Addiction Medicine more power and prestige. " Notice " Motion #1 " below. It is clear that " addiction " can be health problem, and it is also clear that there is no consensus on the meaning of the word.
See
Is Marijuana Addictive? Analysis By Richard Cowan

Consider this from the findings of fact in a recent BC court decision:
" Marihuana is not addictive. "
See
British Columbia Court Rules Two to One That Marijuana Possession Laws Must Be Decided By Parliament. Dissent Makes Hearing By Supreme Court Likely. Facts Make Marijuana Prohibition Look Bad, Again.

Or consider this from the DEAland Institute of Medicine Report:
" A distinctive marijuana withdrawal syndrome has been identified, but it is mild and short-lived. "

Use of marijuana during early adolescence is associated with an increased likelihood of future dependence upon it and other addictive drugs, including cocaine.


(MarijuanaNews note: Consider another of the findings of fact in the recent BC court decision:
 " There is no evidence that marihuana is a gateway drug and the vast majority of marihuana users do not go on to try hard drugs. "

It is certainly true that the earlier children use " drugs, " other than the ubiquitous caffeine, the more likely they are to have substance abuse and other problems. However, it is not clear whether this correlation is caused by the drug use per se, or by the factors that caused and/or allowed the child to use drugs at an early age, i. e., underlying emotional problems, and/or parental neglect -- and/or the social context of marijuana prohibition itself.

In any case, given the huge numbers of adolescents who have used marijuana, and given how few go on to have serious problems, it is clear that the risk is not great, and most teen marijuana users do not suffer serious adverse consequences.

Also, consider the alternatives. If teens use less marijuana, they may well use more alcohol. Would the Addiction Medicine Committee prefer that Canadian adolescents to use alcohol in stead of marijuana? That is not a rhetorical question.


See
Great London Times Column and News From New Zealand Compare Marijuana and Alcohol

Moreover, as the IOM report noted, marijuana is seldom the first drug used. Alcohol and tobacco almost always come first – again after caffeine. The IOM notes that it is the illegality of marijuana that creates the association with hard drug use. " [I]t is the legal status of marijuana that makes it a gateway drug. " It is truly appalling that the BCMA should be clinging to the discredited " gateway theory. " )
See
Prohibitionism After the IOM Report; Analysis by Richard Cowan
and links

Children who smoke marijuana are more likely to drop out of school. There is good evidence to suggest that marijuana use in young people interferes with memory, cognition and successful mastery of the maturational tasks of adolescence. These are disastrous consequences for young people at a crucial stage of preparation for the demands of adulthood.
(MarijuanaNews note: No, " marijuana use " does not cause these problems. Inappropriate and excessive marijuana use may cause such problems, but simply having used marijuana does not. Consider the statement " Aspirin use causes death by internal bleeding. " In fact, aspirin and related drugs – sold over the counter – do cause thousands of such deaths every year.
See
Aspirin And Related Drugs Are 15th Leading Cause Of Death In DEAland
Context For Medical Marijuana

However, aspirin is used safely by millions of people who do not bleed to death. Only those who use too much aspirin – or who are unusually vulnerable to such problems – are at great risk. The same is true of teens and marijuana.

Having laid out a set of questionable premises, the Addiction Medicine Committee modestly says only that the politicians " must take into account " these points. It does not make any specific policy recommendations. Those they can leave to their allies, the Canadian narks. The BCMA should decide on their role in marijuana prohibition. Are they an extension of the police or protectors of the health of their patients?
See
 " It's Time To Declare Peace, " Says Great Canadian Op-ed. But Can Canada Escape the DEAland Marijuana Prohibition Trap, As the Mounties Lie To Keep the War Going? -- 2 items

However, I would like to suggest an alternative resolution:

" The BCMA humbly recognize that being a medical doctor does not make a person an expert in social policies. However, there are some points on which most Canadians can agree. Therefore,

Be it resolved that the BCMA urge the federal and provincial Ministers of Health that in any future parliamentary debate concerning changing the legal status of marijuana, the legislatures must take into account the relative harm caused by various substances and pass laws that have a rational basis in fact.
See
A Proposal For A Rational Allocation Of Drug Education Budgets
Based On The Harm Done By Various Substances -- Analysis By Richard Cowan

There is good evidence that marijuana is much less harmful than alcohol, the most widely abused drug in Canada. Therefore the BCMA urge that Canadian laws should not have the perverse effect of encouraging alcohol use by suppressing the use of a less dangerous drug.
See
The Reality Of the Marijuana Situation In Canada: Unequal Injustice.
Alcohol Costs Canadian Health Almost 100 Times As Much As Marijuana.
Tobacco: Almost 200 As Much – Article and Editorial
and
Criminologist Defends Constable’s Call For Legal Marijuana:
" Alcohol and tobacco much more harmful than cannabis. "

There is overwhelming evidence that alcohol is a highly addictive drug and that its use while driving or working has been shown to increase the likelihood of both motor vehicle accidents and work related accidents, some of them fatal, whereas marijuana has far less negative impact on driving and may actually reduce the tendency of adolescents to drive at excessive speed, a leading cause of accidents. Consequently, while excessive marijuana use may increase the risk of accidents and should be discouraged, there is good evidence that tolerating marijuana use may have the net effect of reducing total accidents, especially if it replaces alcohol.Therefore the BCMA urge that Canadian laws should not discourage a move to social drugs less dangerous than alcohol.
See
Canadian Study Confirms That Marijuana Impairs Driving Far Less Than Alcohol
and links

Inasmuch as the Netherlands has a lower rate of adolescent marijuana and heroin use than does Canada, the BCMA urge that their policies be seriously studied in the development Canadian marijuana policies.
See
Professor Of Medicine At The University Of Toronto Urges Canada To " Go Dutch " At Vancouver Conference On Health, Addictions And Social Justice.

Inasmuch as there is insufficient research on the therapeutic benefits of arresting sick and dying people for using " medical marijuana, " the BCMA urge that this policy be discontinued immediately until a scientific basis for therapeutic arrests can be developed. The BCMA urge Health Canada to begin a five year study comparing the prognosis of sick people in prison with those at home with their families. During this time Canadians who are prescribed cannabis by their physicians should be provided by Health Canada with an adequate supply of medical grade cannabis . This is the only truly scientific way to determine whether arrest and prosecution -- the current policy -- or medical grade cannabis given in a non-punitive context is more beneficial for the sick and dying.
See
British Medical Association Runs A Non-Debate On Medical Marijuana
The Prohibitionist Ignores the Fact That Patients Are Being Arrested
– Unless Court Records Are Just Anecdotal Evidence.

Inasmuch as the BCMACommittee on Violence (See below) urges " developing programs to build capacity in violence prevention " and is concerned about violence in sports, the BCMA also oppose the use of violence against peaceful marijuana users.
See
The Theory and Practice of Chaos – Analysis By Richard Cowan

Inasmuch as having a criminal record has disastrous consequences for young people at a crucial stage of preparation for the demands of adulthood, the BCMA urge that Canadians no longer be subject to arrest for marijuana possession.
See
Ottawa Citizen Practices First Class Journalism
A Brilliantly Insightful Editorial: " Marijuana isn’t just a serious issue. It’s huge. "

Inasmuch as contraband markets do not provide any quality control, and do not prevent marijuana from being sold to youths, and marijuana is sometimes sold in the same distribution channels with much more dangerous drugs, there is good evidence that marijuana prohibition is actually counterproductive and increases the danger to the very youths whom it was supposedly intended to protect. Therefore

the BCMA urge that the Canadian government provide for the legal sale of cannabis products in a way likely to maximize the public health and protect our youth from contraband markets.
See
How the War On Marijuana To Save The Children
Has Become A War On the Children To Save Marijuana Prohibition

Inasmuch as exaggerated statements about the supposed dangers of marijuana are contradicted by the everyday observations of Canadian youths, it is necessary that every effort be made to provide adolescents and parents with accurate information about marijuana and other drugs. The failure to provide accurate information about marijuana undermines the credibility of all substance abuse education. T

herefore the BCMA urge that all government agencies and health organizations take care that all statements about cannabis and other substances be supported by good science.
See
The Need For Drug Prohibition Education.
Analysis By Richard Cowan.
How Can Parents Tell Their Children The Truth In A Sea Of Lies About Marijuana?
and
A Parent Asks,
" Why do institutions that are supposed to be helping kids in trouble feel it necessary to lie to them? "
Inasmuch as the Netherlands provides specialized outpatient treatment to those persons who consider themselves " addicted " to marijuana, the BCMA urge that Health Canada provide such programs without social stigma or the threat of criminal prosecution of the patients.
See
" Tremendous Increase In The Number Of Dutch Cannabis Users Asking For Help "
Swedish Prohibitionists Claim

Inasmuch as the resources being spent on enforcing marijuana prohibition are very substantial and could be better spent on providing for the health needs of Canadians, especially those suffering from the adverse health consequences of alcohol, tobacco and other drugs, the BCMA urge that there be a reconsideration of budgetary priorities.

The BCMA regrets the role that it has played, both by omission and commission, in denying the people of Canada the medical benefits of marijuana and of a rational drugs policy. "

Other Motions and resolutions proposed by...

Addiction Medicine Committee

Motion #1:

Be it resolved that the BCMA once again urge the Premier, the Minister of Health and the Minister of Children and Families to identify sufficient resources to create an independent body composed of experts and representatives of those affected, directly responsible to the legislature and the Premier. This body, independent from political influence, would be responsible for making recommendations to government with respect to:

  • Policies affecting availability, pricing, sales, and provincial statutes concerning addictive substances;

  • Research into prevention and treatment of addictive disorders;

  • Screening for and intervention on substance use disorders in various settings;

  • Treatment programs and resources.

British Columbia has gone from having a comprehensive program of research, prevention and a range of treatment modalities for substance use disorders to it’s current state of having large gaps in the continuum of addiction services. Numerous organizations and reports, including the BCMA TASC Report, No Further Harm, have called for the creation of an organization, representing affected parties and expert opinion, to oversee the advancement of research and evidence-based prevention, intervention and treatment of substance use disorders and development of policy recommendations for this province.

Committee on Tobacco & Illness

Motion #1:

Be it resolved that the BCMA strongly urge the Government of B.C.,

to add 12 cents per pack (and the equivalent in roll-your-own cigarette tobacco) to the price of cigarettes sold in this Province; or

if the Government is unwilling to increase cigarette taxes, then 5% of all the money derived by the Province from taxing cigarettes should be used for the following two funds:

  1. a smokers’ assistance fund to help smokers defray the cost of proven clinical tobacco interventions*

  2. a clinical tobacco cessation fund to pay providers of tobacco intervention.

*proven as defined by randomized clinical trials,

summarized by Therapeutic Initiative (UBC), the Cochrane Collection, and the US AHCPR Clinical Practice Guideline #18.

Severe addiction to cigarettes

is not an equal-opportunity addiction (being determined by genetics, education level and tobacco-industry marketing);

and

Clinical tobacco intervention is highly cost effective and grossly under resourced.

Motion #2

Be it resolved that the BCMA write to all city and town councils in British Columbia and to all regional health boards to encourage implementing local ordinances to prohibit smoking in all adult venues and long-term care facilities.

The Supreme Court struck down section 4.83(3) of the Workers' Compensation Boards' Occupational Safety and Health Regulation. The decision has the effect of reinstituting an exemption from the general requirements of employers to controlling exposure of workers to Environmental Tobacco Smoke (ETS) in the public area of certain facilities such as bars and long term residential care facilities. The judge found that the board exceeded its powers in instituting a " sunset clause " without holding proper public hearings.

No health authorities in North America have found ventilation to be an acceptable solution. ASHRAE, the American Society of Heating, Refrigeration, and Air Conditioning Engineers, the organization that sets ventilation standards in North America, twice rejected in June and September, 1999 a request by the organization representing BC pub owners to state that ventilation could manage the air pollution that comes from 2nd hand cigarette smoke.

Despite the WCB’s initiative being overturned, the principle of a smoke free workplace is supported. Standardization of regulations across Municipal boundaries makes sense and is needed. With the Provincial Government failing to implement a province-wide ban, the Municipal Governments must act on this issue.

Committee on Violence

Motion #1:

Be it resolved that the BCMA work with OHSAH, where appropriate in developing programs to build capacity in violence prevention, including training programs and train the trainer programs, suitable to a wide variety of healthcare settings.

Healthcare workers are entitled to a safe and secure workplace,

and both the BC Medical Association and the Occupational Health and Safety Agency for Healthcare (OHSAH), representing employers and the healthcare workforce, share this mission.

Motion #3:

Be it resolved that violent acts outside the rules of the sport by its participants be treated by the law as if the violence occurred outside of sport.
